doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: Meeting Sun Ra in Chicago in 1959
summary: Griffin explains the 1958 savings lost to bailing out a friend, then hears Sun Ra's band rehearsing in Chicago in 1959 and is invited to play.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Wow. Wonderful. Let me move you up to summers in Chicago and if my sources are correct you’re walking down the street and you hear what turned out to be Sun Ra?

Yeah. That was interesting. So my whole career kind of started in 1959. In ’58 I graduated from high school, my good mother — I would save my money. I was very good at saving. I majored in business in high school. I learned a lot about money. Thank God I’ve been able to apply — to stay on the right end of money you know. And so I had saved a hundred dollars, I remember very clearly. ’58 was supposed to be the year that I would go to Chicago and when I went, if I had gone in ’58 it would have been the first time that I’ve never seen the sign that says “colored” and “white” and “white water fountain” and everything. I would be able to go across the Mason-Dixon line. So my friend, God rest his soul, Paul Woods got put in jail for drinking. You know? He got arrested, he was inebriated. So my mother, being her good soul, “You’ve got to get Paul out.” So my money that I had saved a whole year, I bailed Paul out and do you know two weeks later Paul was back in jail but anyway that’s spoiled my whole summer. I was very, you know like frugal or whatever. I saved. I wouldn’t spend money on anything that I didn’t think was absolutely necessary. So anyway ’59 I finally did the same thing, saved my money and went to Chicago. And I had an aunt who was very strict. She had a curfew. You know I’m 19 years old in Chicago, Chicago is a rough city, I’m down from Jackson, Mississippi. I wouldn’t be able to survive in Chicago. But she didn’t know that I

had been around a lot of the criminals and street people — I wouldn’t say criminals, a lot of people that were on the funny side of the law and knew how to hustle and all that stuff. So I was very aware to a certain extent of what the street was like. But she said, “Okay you’ve got to be in after 7 o’clock or dark. So I was walking in the street in Chicago and I heard live music and you know I was definitely into music, I played in clubs and all that stuff. So I walked in and there was Sun Ra, there was Marshall Allen, Pat Patrick, John Gilmore, Ronnie Boykins and I’m not sure of the drummer, but so they were playing, they were rehearsing. I said ooh — and their music was very interesting and exciting ‘cause you know I’d been listening to jazz on records but I hadn’t heard anything like what Sun Ra was doing. So, and he — with his mild manner — and he said, “Hello, how are you doing?” and he’d nod. I said, “I play the trombone.” He said, “Grab your horn and come to play with us tomorrow.” And that’s what I did. And I could read music. So Ronnie Boykins and I would do duets. He played the bass. And those musicians was well trained. I mean Marshall to the day is so good at sight reading, and he had played in Paris because he just turned 99 — he had played in Paris when Josephine Baker was over there — not that he played, but Marshall goes very deep. And he had just gotten out of the Army around that time. I think he got out — he joined the band in ’58 and Julian Priester joined the band in ’56 and Charles Davis, the late Charles Davis, he was around, he and Julian Priester got in the band around the same time. I’m not sure when James Spaulding was in the band but he’s still with us. So ain’t but a handful of people, I would say maybe four or five at the most, that go back as deep as Marshall and Julian Priester and myself played in the band.
